clue.text: Marsupial reproductive organ initially astounded taxonomists

parts.note: the organ a mammal carries its unborn young in

indicators.note: what is done initially is done at the very start, so only the opening letter of each word beside it is taken

parts.note: the initial letters of the two words, in the order the clue prints them

explanation.walkthrough: A marsupial's young finish growing in the pouch rather than the womb, so the organ the wordplay borrows is the one this animal makes least use of.
explanation.definitionFit: Marsupial -> WOMBAT: definition by example, since the wombat is one particular Australian pouched animal and the clue names only the family.

clue.text: Burmese boarding houses served up super roly-poly

indicators.note: to house something is to keep it within your walls, so these words have the answer indoors
a dish comes up from the kitchen, and in a down entry coming up means reading from the bottom square towards the top

parts.note: the tail of the first word and the head of the second give five letters in a row, and they read the right way only from the far end

explanation.walkthrough: A roly-poly is a suet pudding as well as a shape, which is what lets a boarding-house dinner and a description of a diner share one sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: super roly-poly -> OBESE: roly-poly is the nursery word for comfortably round, and pushing it to 'super' reaches the clinical term for dangerously overweight.

clue.text: Stupid Scandinavian spawned Spoonerism

indicators.note: the clue says outright that the opening sounds of the two words are to be swapped

parts.note: a Dane is a Scandinavian, a person from Denmark
bred means spawned, produced offspring

explanation.surface: A Scandinavian gave rise to the Spoonerism, as if the Revd Spooner had been Danish.
explanation.walkthrough: DANE is said like DAIN and BRED like BREAD; the 'Spoonerism' swaps their opening sounds, D and BR, giving the hyphenated answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Brain-dead is an informal insult for someone extremely dim or foolish.

clue.text: Hunter S dismissed as gossip?

indicators.note: dismissed means sent away, so the letter S is dropped from the hunter word

parts.note: a stalker is a hunter who creeps up on prey, especially deer

explanation.surface: It looks like the writer Hunter S. Thompson being written off as a mere tittle-tattler.
explanation.walkthrough: Hunter S. Thompson was the American gonzo journalist; here Hunter means STALKER and the S is the letter to remove.
explanation.definitionFit: A talker is a chatterer, and a gossip is one kind of talker, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Troublemakers playing REM single endlessly

indicators.note: playing as in playing around with, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: endlessly means the word single loses its last letter

parts.note: without its final E it gives SINGL

explanation.surface: Mischief-makers are blasting out a single by the rock band REM over and over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endlessly' looks like it means on repeat, but it trims single to SINGL, which 'playing' mixes with REM.
explanation.definitionFit: Gremlins are imaginary imps blamed for mechanical faults, so they cause trouble.

clue.text: Enraged MAGA chants meet defending Democrat's victory statement

indicators.note: the rearranged letters surround and so defend the Democrat letter
enraged suggests wild disorder, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written
D is the abbreviation for a Democrat in US politics

explanation.surface: Angry Trump supporters chanting at a rally face off against a Democrat.
explanation.walkthrough: MAGA is Trump's Make America Great Again slogan; its letters with CHANTS and MEET are rearranged around D.
explanation.definitionFit: The tennis umpire's call game, set and match announces a win, and it is used generally to mean decisive victory.

clue.text: Cries of former international comprehended by reticent people

parts.note: an ex is a former partner, and EX- is the standing prefix for anything former

indicators.note: in its older sense to comprehend is to take something in and hold it, so the piece beside it swallows the other

parts.note: someone who clams up refuses to say anything, so a clam is a reticent person
an international is a player capped for their country, and I is the abbreviation for it; it lands between the A and the M

explanation.walkthrough: Reticent people who make cries of any kind are a contradiction, and the clue survives it because the two halves never meet: one is the definition, the other the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Cries -> EXCLAIMS: to exclaim is to cry out suddenly, so the definition is the everyday verb for the same short burst of speech.

clue.text: Odd characters fleeing flood in Rye Valley

indicators.note: number the letters along and let the first, third and fifth run away; every second one is left standing

parts.note: ten letters, of which the second, fourth, sixth, eighth and tenth stay behind

explanation.walkthrough: Rye is a Sussex town where flooding is a real worry, so the surface reads as local news while the letters are quietly being counted off in French.
explanation.definitionFit: Valley -> LOIRE: the Loire Valley is the chateau-lined stretch of central France, known to everyone by the river's name alone.

clue.text: Drunken bum slunk around Lima? Idiot!

indicators.note: the rearranged letters go around the Lima letter
drunken means reeling, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
Lima is L in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A drunk layabout skulks around the streets of Lima, Peru, and someone shouts an insult.
explanation.walkthrough: Lima looks like the Peruvian capital, which the question mark plays on, but it stands for L in the radio alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: A numbskull is a stupid person, a dolt.

clue.text: Lament extremely bizarre rule about nursing institute

indicators.note: extremely points to the extremes of the word bizarre, its first and last letters

parts.note: its outer letters are B and E

indicators.note: nursing means holding something close, so the reversed rule holds the institute letter
about here means turned around, so the word for rule is read backwards

parts.note: a law is a rule

explanation.surface: Someone grumbles about a very strange regulation concerning a nursing institute.
explanation.definitionFit: To bewail something is to express great sorrow over it, which is exactly what lamenting does.

clue.text: Chairman maintains church is centre of harmful masculinity

indicators.note: to maintain something is to keep hold of it, so this word keeps the others inside itself

parts.note: Chairman Mao ruled China from 1949, and the title alone is enough to name him
CH is what an Ordnance Survey map prints for a church

indicators.note: the centre of a word is the letter with the same number standing either side of it

parts.note: the verb is taken at face value, two letters as written
the middle letter of the seven, with three on each side

explanation.walkthrough: 'Harmful masculinity' is the phrase the surface wants read whole, and prising it apart is the solve: only the second word is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: masculinity -> MACHISMO: the Spanish word for aggressive male pride, taken into English for masculinity of the strutting, something-to-prove kind.

clue.text: Turns nasty colour, repulsed by sulphur

parts.note: a mean trick is a nasty one

indicators.note: an attack that is repulsed is driven straight back the way it came, and so are these three letters

parts.note: the plainest colour of them all, and it arrives back to front
S is sulphur's symbol in the periodic table

explanation.walkthrough: 'Turns nasty' is a phrase, and separating the two words is the whole clue: one of them is the definition and the other is four letters of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Turns -> MEANDERS: a river that meanders turns this way and that across flat ground, so the verb names continual wandering rather than one bend.

clue.text: Opposed state surveillance on vacation

parts.note: to aver something is to state it firmly, a word that survives mostly in court

indicators.note: a house whose owners are on vacation is empty in the middle, with only its outside left standing

parts.note: everything between its first letter and its last has gone away, leaving the two ends

explanation.walkthrough: 'State surveillance' is one idea on the surface and two separate jobs underneath, which is why a clue about spying reads so much like a headline.
explanation.definitionFit: Opposed -> AVERSE: to be averse to a thing is to be set against it, and the word almost always arrives with 'to' in front of what is opposed.

clue.text: District of Cadiz on escarpment

indicators.note: a district of a place is a piece taken from inside it, and this piece is taken from inside the words that follow

parts.note: the four letters run across the joins, from the end of the Spanish port into the start of the slope

explanation.walkthrough: Cadiz and an escarpment make a plausible piece of geography, and geography is the one thing they are not doing here: they are only lending letters.
explanation.definitionFit: District -> ZONE: a zone is an area marked off and treated as a single unit, so it is the planner's word for what everyday speech calls a district.

clue.text: Deference award one kept in study overlooking empty countryside

indicators.note: in a down clue, overlooking means sitting above, so these pieces come before what follows

parts.note: the OBE is a British honour, Officer of the Order of the British Empire

indicators.note: kept in means placed inside, so the one goes into the study

parts.note: a den is a private room for study or work
I is the Roman numeral one

indicators.note: empty means the inside of the word is removed, leaving only its first and last letters

parts.note: emptied, it leaves C and E

explanation.surface: A medal-winner respected for having studied while gazing out over a deserted landscape.
explanation.walkthrough: 'overlooking' works because this is a down entry: the award and the study come above the emptied countryside.
explanation.definitionFit: Obedience is compliance with the wishes of others, the same submissive respect that deference describes.

clue.text: Fearful rodent discovered on Southeast Asian island

indicators.note: in an across clue, one piece written on another follows it

parts.note: Timor is an island in Southeast Asia, shared by Indonesia and East Timor

indicators.note: dis-covered: the rodent loses its covering, its outer letters

parts.note: a mouse is a rodent

explanation.surface: A frightened rodent turns up on an island in the Indonesian archipelago.
explanation.walkthrough: 'discovered' looks like found, but read as dis-covered it strips MOUSE to OUS.
explanation.definitionFit: Timorous means timid and easily frightened, which is fearful.

clue.text: Drag one's feet following concerning shake-up

indicators.note: what follows a thing comes after it, and in a down entry after means further down the column

parts.note: RE heads a memo to mean concerning, from the Latin for 'in the matter of'
to shuffle is to walk without lifting your feet clear of the floor

explanation.walkthrough: 'Shake-up' sits at the end of the clue looking like an instruction to rearrange letters. It is the definition, and nothing in this one gets rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: shake-up -> RESHUFFLE: a cabinet reshuffle moves the same people into different jobs, which is exactly what a shake-up of an organisation amounts to.

clue.text: Pinch child squashing tiny insect

indicators.note: to squash a thing is to press down until it is flat under whatever is on top, so the piece named next ends up buried

parts.note: a son is somebody's child, and the word opens up after its first letter
the biting fly of Scottish summers, small enough to fit inside

explanation.walkthrough: A child squashing an insect is a complete small scene, and it does the opposite of what it says: the insect ends up inside the child, entirely intact.
explanation.definitionFit: Pinch -> SMIDGEON: a pinch of salt is as much as finger and thumb will hold, and a smidgeon is the same vague, very small helping.

clue.text: Detective entertained by Melville's name for bucolic character

indicators.note: a host entertains a guest inside the house, so the letters beside it take the other piece in

parts.note: the author of Moby-Dick was Herman Melville, and his first name parts after three letters
DS is a detective sergeant's rank as the police abbreviate it

explanation.walkthrough: Whale-hunting is nobody's idea of a pastoral scene, which makes Melville's own name a good place to keep a man who looks after cattle.
explanation.definitionFit: bucolic character -> HERDSMAN: bucolic means of the countryside and its herding life, so the figure the word conjures is the one driving the cattle.

clue.text: Piece one played very softly in auditorium

indicators.note: an auditorium is a room for hearing, so whatever happens there reaches you through the ear rather than the eye

parts.note: to play very softly is to play so low, and the two words run together into one when you say them

explanation.walkthrough: Music sits on both sides of this clue, a dynamic marking on one and a performance on the other, so the ear is the only thing keeping them apart.
explanation.definitionFit: Piece one played -> SOLO: a solo is written for a single performer, so the definition names it by counting the people on stage.

clue.text: Seek over-the-counter drug when lacking in energy

indicators.note: lacking says the drug name is without the letters of the next word

parts.note: aspirin is a painkiller sold over the counter, without a prescription
taken as written, the letters to remove
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: Someone looks for a painkiller from the pharmacy when feeling low on energy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lacking in energy' reads as tired, but 'in' is the letters taken from ASPIRIN, and energy adds E.
explanation.definitionFit: To aspire is to aim at or strive for something, which is seeking it.

clue.text: Funny bone with a large diameter

parts.note: one of the twelve pairs curving round the chest
the article is taken exactly as printed
L is the size printed on a clothing label
d stands for diameter in a geometry formula

explanation.walkthrough: 'Funny bone' is the phrase the surface offers and its two words belong to opposite halves of the clue, which is as neat a join as this grid has.
explanation.definitionFit: Funny -> RIBALD: ribald humour is the coarse, rude sort, so the definition offers the mildest available word for a joke that is anything but.

clue.text: An epoch reflected in entertainment venue

indicators.note: a reflection shows a thing the wrong way round, and these five letters are read back out of the mirror

parts.note: the article is taken exactly as printed, two letters
an era is a stretch of history, the epoch of a geologist or a historian

explanation.walkthrough: Five letters that read as an ordinary scrap of English forwards and a concert venue backwards; the surface is doing nothing but supplying them.
explanation.definitionFit: entertainment venue -> ARENA: the Roman arena was the sanded floor where the spectacle took place, and the word now covers the whole building a tour plays in.

clue.text: Times desperately stifling question over inaccurate citation

indicators.note: stifling means smothering, so the rearranged Times letters close around the others
desperately suggests a frantic mess, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
O is the cricket scoring abbreviation for an over

explanation.surface: The Times newspaper anxiously suppresses an awkward query.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram of TIMES splits as MIS and TE around QUO.
explanation.definitionFit: To misquote is to cite words wrongly; here the noun means a quotation given incorrectly.

clue.text: Seduce office worker close to retirement

parts.note: a temp is the agency worker brought in to cover a desk for a week

indicators.note: the close of anything is its end, so only the final letter of the word beside it is wanted

parts.note: the letter the word closes on

explanation.walkthrough: An office worker close to retirement is a whole person in five words, and the clue needs you to stop seeing them and start counting letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Seduce -> TEMPT: both mean drawing someone towards what they should resist, tempt being the older and milder of the two, as in tempting fate.

clue.text: Entire broadcast about New Hampshire native

indicators.note: the rearranged letters go about, around, the state abbreviation
broadcast as in scattered about, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
NH is the postal abbreviation for New Hampshire

explanation.surface: A whole radio programme is broadcast about the US state of New Hampshire.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram of ENTIRE splits as IN and ERENT around NH.
explanation.definitionFit: An inherent quality is inborn or intrinsic, which is what native means of a talent or trait.

clue.text: Popular fellow beginning to appreciate setter's notoriety

parts.note: whatever is in this season is what is popular

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is the letter it starts with, and that is all this one contributes

parts.note: F is the abbreviation for fellow, as after the name of a Royal Society member
the first letter of the word
the setter is the voice writing the clue, so anything of the setter's is mine

explanation.walkthrough: 'Setter's' means 'my' wherever a crossword says it — the setter speaks the clue in the first person — and it is one of the earliest conventions worth owning.
explanation.definitionFit: notoriety -> INFAMY: infamy is fame gone bad, so the definition is the neutral-sounding noun for being widely known for the wrong reasons.

clue.text: A filling meal after essentially free promotional event

indicators.note: after means the filled meal follows the middle of free
essentially points to the essence or heart of the word free, its middle letters

parts.note: its middle letters are R and E

indicators.note: filling means going inside, so A sits within the meal

parts.note: lunch is a meal

explanation.surface: A sponsored free lunch handed out at a marketing launch.
explanation.definitionFit: A relaunch is a fresh marketing launch of a product, an occasion staged to publicise it.

clue.text: Releases tip of willie caught in flies!

indicators.note: the tip of a thing is its far end, so what is wanted is the letter the word finishes on

parts.note: the letter at the very end of the word

indicators.note: whatever is caught in something is held inside it, so this letter sits among the others rather than beside them

parts.note: jets are aircraft, so 'flies' is a noun here and not a verb
c is how a cricket scorecard records a batsman caught, and it drops in after the second letter

explanation.walkthrough: The seaside-postcard surface is the joke, and every word of it turns out respectable: a trouser zip, some aircraft and a line of a cricket score.
explanation.definitionFit: Releases -> EJECTS: a machine ejects a cassette by pushing it out, so the definition is the gentler word for the same forcible letting-go.
